doc.title: Nick Brignola interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 28, 1997

title: Rhythm and blues bands, the trapeze act and learning by sitting in
summary: He played R&B at Sylvan Beach and on the road, swung on a trapeze with The Goofers, learned from Jimmy Cavallo, and used gigs and jam sessions as his schooling.

bands.name: Jimmy Cavallo and the House Rockers

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Well there was a lot of different kinds of music happening in the 50s. Did you get into, either by economic necessity or whatever, get into—
I got into all of it, believe me. You’re from around here, right?
Okay. Are you familiar with Sylvan Beach?

Okay. I played there when I was a kid with a rhythm & blues band. In fact in re-hashing those years with people that know me and musicians from around here, I realize that we were all kind of doing the same thing but didn’t know each other. Because I came from Albany basically. But I played rhythm & blues, I played — I actually swung from a trapeze upside-down playing alto.

Oh, yeah. We were on the road and there was a group that used to appear on The Ed Sullivan Show, they were Las Vegas’s biggest act, they were called “The Goofers.” And they played rhythm & blues and they did comedy and everything. But one of the gimmicks was the sax player would swing on a trapeze. So we were playing in St. Louis and the guy had left his trapeze. So I got on it so I was fooling around and the guy says, “You think you can do that tonight?” And I said, “I’ll try.” Well that lasted about a week, because I got dizzy a few times and almost killed myself so I never got on the trapeze again. But there was another guy that came from this area — Jimmy Cavallo and the House Rockers. And Jimmy showed me how to “walk the bar.” You know, so I did all of that. But Rhythm & Blues enabled me to learn how to — it put me in a situation where I could improvise and just blow anything I want. In other words I’d be up there kind of

thinking and hearing Paul Desmond, but I’d be honking, and I’d be playing all those harmonic things I heard the Claude Thornhill band play when we’re playing like some current rock tune from the day. Like “Rock Around the Clock” by Bill Haiey is nothing but a blues, right? So once we played the head and started to blow, I just blew. I was Sonny Rollins at that point you know. But I learned how to play that way and then I used to go and sit in at jam sessions and in strange towns and learn tunes and sit in with people and that’s kind of how I learned to play. That was school for me.
